Rugged tablet for PlanRadar

PlanRadar is construction and property documentation software from PlanRadar GmbH, a Vienna company that lists a London office at 79-81 Borough Road on its contact page and prices in pounds on its UK site. The vendor describes it as one platform for project documentation, processes and reporting: tasks and defects are recorded as tickets pinned to a digital plan or a BIM model, with photos, text, voice messages and documents attached, and the same tickets feed site diaries, snag lists, inspection forms and handover reports exported as PDF or Excel. The office works in the web app in a browser; the site team works in the mobile app.

The vendor's own help centre draws that line clearly. The web app is described as optimised for back office work, reporting, statistics and account setup, and it cannot take new photos, videos or voice recordings, only upload existing files. The mobile app is where tickets are created on site, where GPS positions are added, where QR codes and NFC tags open tickets, and where work carries on without a connection and syncs later. That is a device that gets carried round a half-built floor plate, held up against a wall to photograph a defect, and used in the rain on an external inspection, which is a hard life for a consumer tablet.

This page sets out what PlanRadar publishes about the devices its apps run on, which Tuga rugged tablets meet those published figures, where the Windows app fits and what the vendor says it does not do, and how a UK contractor or facilities team can buy a single trial unit before kitting out a wider team.

Requirements

What PlanRadar needs from a device

Each item below comes from PlanRadar GmbH's own listing or documentation, with the source linked.

  • Android 10 with a minimum of 4GB RAM; the help centre adds a rolling support policy

    The vendor's System Requirements and Security page lists the Android app for smartphones and tablets as requiring Android 10 with a minimum of 4GB RAM, and the iOS app as requiring iOS 16 or later. Its help centre System Requirements article (updated 26 August 2026) states a different, rolling rule: for iOS and Android we always support the two latest major operating system versions. It does not name those versions. It also says iOS and Android tablets with access to the App Store or Play Store can be used to install and run the mobile app. Because the two pages differ, treat Android 10 and 4GB as the published floor and check the help centre before buying for a long service life. Source: planradar.com

  • Android app from Google Play, for phones and tablets

    The Android app is published on Google Play as PlanRadar Construction Manager (package com.defectradar, developer PlanRadar GmbH). When checked on 19 October 2026 the listing showed version 14.3.0, updated 11 October 2026, a Requires Android figure of 7.0, more than 1,000,000 downloads, and device chips for Phone and Tablet. The help centre's download section links to this listing for Android and to the App Store for iOS, where the listing showed iOS 17.0 or iPadOS 17.0 or later at the time of checking. The Play Store floor of Android 7.0 is lower than the vendor's own published Android 10, and the vendor's figure is the one to plan on. Source: play.google.com

  • More than 32GB of internal storage, and 8GB RAM for BIM

    The help centre System Requirements article gives a minimum internal storage of more than 32GB and recommends mobile devices with a lot of internal storage, because the need depends on your projects. Its estimates are about 350MB for the Android app before any project data, about 350MB for 1,000 pictures, about 700MB for 100 plans and about 1GB for 10 BIM models. For BIM it asks for modern devices with a fast GPU and CPU and a minimum of 8GB of RAM, and the separate BIM Support article (updated 24 August 2026) says models are synced to the mobile apps for offline use and suggests 16GB of RAM or more for larger models. No processor model or screen size is published for the mobile app. Source: help.planradar.com

  • Offline working in the mobile app, with a sync before you lose signal

    The Working Offline article says you must be logged in to work offline and should sync regularly, especially before going somewhere with poor or no connectivity; syncing downloads tickets, ticket attachments and plans to the app. Offline you can browse synced projects, plans and tickets, and view, edit and create tickets. Changes made offline are not visible to other users until the app is opened with an active connection, when they are pushed to the server automatically. Syncing a single project rather than all projects is currently iOS only, not Android. The quick start guide says a first sync might take a few minutes and the app should stay open until it finishes. Documents can be marked Make available offline. The vendor does not document offline working for the web app. Source: help.planradar.com

  • QR codes and NFC tags to open tickets: camera scanning, iOS and Android apps only, Pro and Enterprise plans

    The QR code article says the feature is available to Pro and Enterprise accounts and is only available on the iOS and Android apps. It is switched on in the app's Settings, and scanning uses the in-app scanner, which opens the camera from the search icon in the ticket list or plan view, with a flashlight toggle for dark areas; on Android the device's own camera app can also read the code and open the link. QR codes must be ordered with information supplied by PlanRadar, or they will not work with the app. The NFC article, also Pro and Enterprise, says the device must support reading and writing NFC tags, that tags must be NDEF, writable and at least 100 bytes, and that on Android the feature is enabled in the app settings with NFC turned on in the Android settings. No dedicated hardware scan engine and no external scanner is documented. Source: help.planradar.com

  • GPS positions on tickets, and photos, video and voice captured in the mobile app

    The Add GPS Position to Tickets in the Mobile App article (updated 29 October 2025) says GPS must be enabled on the device, the app must be allowed to add GPS positions in its Application Settings, and the ticket form must have Geographical Location switched on. Adding, editing and removing a position is done in the mobile app; the web app only displays it. The quick start guide for in-house users says photos, videos of up to 2 minutes, one voice recording per ticket and documents can be added to tickets from the mobile app, and that the web app only supports uploading existing documents and media files. No location accuracy figure is published. Source: help.planradar.com

  • Windows: a Microsoft Store app for Windows 10 or later, with the vendor saying not all features are supported

    The vendor's quick start welcome page links a Windows download to the Microsoft Store, where the listing (product 9NRWNZW8400X, publisher PlanRadar GmbH, last updated 22 May 2026) gives a minimum of Windows 10 version 17763.0 or higher, x64 architecture, available on PC, and recommends an integrated camera. The System Requirements and Security page lists Windows 10 tablets with the note that not all features are supported and that to use all features you should use an iOS or Android device. The current help centre articles on system requirements, the app overview and BIM support describe iOS, Android and the web app only. The web app itself runs in any modern browser, with the latest Chrome recommended, at a minimum resolution of 1024 x 768 and a recommended 1440 x 900 (figures from the help centre system requirements article in the sources below). Source: planradar.com

Worth knowing. PlanRadar publishes a Windows app on the Microsoft Store, but its requirements page says not all features are supported on Windows tablets and directs users to iOS or Android for the full set, and its current help centre articles describe iOS, Android and the web app only. The QR code and NFC ticket features are documented for the iOS and Android apps, and GPS positions for the mobile app, so the Tuga W10 suits a site office desk running the web app rather than the person walking the floor. On the Android side, the only scan method the vendor documents is the camera, so the A6's Zebra 2D scan engine is not a documented PlanRadar input. The Tuga A6's 4GB of RAM meets the published 4GB minimum exactly, with no margin, and both the A6 and the A8 sit below the 8GB of RAM the help centre asks for on BIM. The vendor's two requirement pages differ: one gives Android 10, the other a rolling policy of the two latest major versions without naming them, and the Google Play listing accepts Android 7.0, so check the help centre before buying for a long service life. The vendor publishes no processor, screen size or location accuracy figure for the mobile app, and the QR code and NFC features need a Pro or Enterprise plan.
Setting up

Getting PlanRadar running

  1. Ask your PlanRadar administrator to invite the user to the account with a role that can create and edit tickets, and to add the projects, plans and forms (including the site diary form) they will need on site.
  2. On the Tuga A10, A8 or A6, open Google Play and install PlanRadar Construction Manager (package com.defectradar, developer PlanRadar GmbH), then sign in. Allow camera, location and notification access when the app asks.
  3. Before the first visit, open the main menu and tap Sync with All projects selected, and keep the app open until it finishes; the vendor says a first sync might take a few minutes. Mark any documents you need in the Documents section as Make available offline.
  4. In the app's Settings, turn on Add GPS Position to Tickets, and on Pro or Enterprise plans turn on the QR code feature and the NFC feature. For NFC, also switch NFC on in the Android settings and test a sample tag before buying a batch, as the vendor recommends.
  5. Order QR codes using the information PlanRadar support supplies, because the vendor says codes ordered without it will not work with the app. Test the in-app scanner on one code and the flashlight toggle in a dark plant room.
  6. Complete a test ticket on a plan with a photo, a voice note and a GPS position, then put the device in flight mode, create a second ticket, and confirm both sync when you come back online.
  7. On a Tuga W10, install PlanRadar from the Microsoft Store or open the web app in Edge or Chrome, and use it for reports, project setup and user management. Check the features your team needs on it before relying on it on site, since the vendor says not all features are supported on Windows.
  8. For the A10 and A8, fit the vehicle mounting dock in the van; for the A10 and W10, add the charging dock where devices live overnight; for the A6, add the belt holster. Fit the tempered glass screen protector before the device goes out.

Questions

PlanRadar on a Tuga device

PlanRadar's requirements page publishes Android 10 with a minimum of 4GB RAM, its help centre asks for more than 32GB of internal storage and 8GB of RAM for BIM, and its Google Play listing gives a Requires Android figure of 7.0 with Phone and Tablet device chips. The Tuga A10 runs Android 14 with Google Play and has 8GB RAM and 128GB storage, so it meets each published figure, including the BIM one. The Tuga A8 (Android 12, 6GB RAM, 128GB) meets the general figures but not the 8GB BIM recommendation, and the Tuga A6 (Android 15, 4GB RAM, 64GB) meets the 4GB minimum with no headroom. We do not describe any device as certified or tested by PlanRadar; these are the vendor's published figures set against the device specifications. The help centre also states a rolling policy of supporting the two latest major Android versions without naming them, so check it before buying for a long service life.

Yes, in the mobile app, provided you sync first. The vendor's Working Offline article says you must be logged in, that syncing downloads tickets, attachments and plans to the app, and that offline you can browse synced projects and plans and view, edit and create tickets. Changes made offline are pushed to the server automatically once the app is opened with a connection, and until then other users cannot see them. The A10, A8 and A6 all run the Google Play app. The vendor does not document offline working for the web app, and its current help centre articles do not describe the Windows app, so on a Tuga W10 check offline behaviour yourself before relying on it.

On Pro and Enterprise plans, yes. The vendor's QR code article says the feature is only available on the iOS and Android apps and that the in-app scanner opens the camera, with a flashlight toggle for dark areas; QR codes must be ordered with information PlanRadar supplies. The NFC article says the device must support reading and writing NDEF tags and that on Android the feature is enabled in the app settings with NFC turned on. The A10, A8 and A6 all have NFC and a 13MP rear camera with flash, and on each of them QR scanning runs through the camera via the app. The A6 also has a Zebra 2D scan engine, but the vendor documents no dedicated scan engine or external scanner, so do not buy it for that reason alone.

Only if the main job is the web app in a site office. The Windows app is on the Microsoft Store with a minimum of Windows 10 version 17763.0 on x64, which the Tuga W10's Windows 11 Pro meets, but the vendor's requirements page says not all features are supported on Windows tablets and tells you to use an iOS or Android device for all of them. QR code and NFC ticket links are documented for the iOS and Android apps only, GPS positions for the mobile app, and the current help centre articles on requirements, the app overview and BIM describe iOS, Android and the web app without mentioning Windows. The W10 does bring Ethernet, HDMI and a desktop browser for reports, project setup and user management, so a team with one site office desk and several people on the floor is usually better served by a W10 at the desk and A10s on site.

Both meet PlanRadar's published Android and RAM figures. The A10 has 8GB RAM against 6GB, which matters because the help centre asks for 8GB on BIM, a sharper 1920 x 1200 screen for reading drawings and placing tickets on them, IP68 against IP67, and MIL-STD-810H, which the A8 does not have. The A8 has a 1000 nit screen against the A10's 350 nits, a removable battery, VESA mount points, and costs £379 against £449. Staff who spend the day on external inspections in bright light, or who want a one-handed device, may prefer the A8; those working from drawings or BIM models, or in wetter and harder conditions, are better served by the A10.
